chapters.title: Chapter 1: What a Trade War Actually Is

lessons.title: Tariffs, Sanctions, and Currency Wars: The Building Blocks of a Trade War

children.text: In August 2025, the United States raised tariffs on a wide range of Indian exports, garments, shrimp, gems and jewellery, to 50%. Half of that was a standard reciprocal tariff. The other half was a penalty, imposed specifically because India kept buying discounted Russian crude oil after the Ukraine invasion. That single move captured all three tools a country reaches for in a trade war: a tariff (the base 25%), a sanction-style penalty tied to foreign policy (the additional 25% over Russian oil purchases), and pressure that rippled straight into how the Reserve Bank of India manages the rupee.

If you trade Indian equities or run a portfolio with export-heavy names, understanding these three tools individually is the first step to reading a trade war instead of just reacting to the headline. A trade war is not one single action. It is an escalating exchange of retaliatory economic measures between two or more countries, each trying to pressure the other without going to actual war. Governments reach for three main levers: tariffs, sanctions, and currency policy. Most real trade wars mix all three. Knowing which lever is being pulled tells you which part of the market feels it first.

children.text: A tariff is a tax a government charges on goods coming into the country. The most common form is an

, a percentage of the good's declared value, charged at the border when the shipment clears customs. If an Indian exporter ships goods worth ₹1 crore to the US and faces a 50% tariff, the US importer owes an extra ₹50 lakh to customs before the shipment is released. That cost gets split in practice: some is absorbed by the exporter cutting its price, some is passed on to the American buyer, and some simply makes the order unprofitable, so it stops altogether. Tariffs are applied at the product category level, classified by
, so a single country's exports can face very different tariff rates depending on whether the shipment is machinery, textiles, or pharmaceuticals.

children.text: A sanction is a restriction on trade, finance, or access to a country's own assets, used as a foreign policy weapon rather than a revenue-raising one. Sanctions can freeze a government's foreign currency reserves, block its banks from the SWIFT international payments network, or ban specific individuals and companies from doing business globally. After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the US and its allies froze roughly $300 billion of Russian central bank reserves held abroad and cut several major Russian banks off from SWIFT. India did not join these sanctions and continued buying discounted Russian crude, which Indian refiners processed and, in some cases, re-exported as refined fuel. That trade pattern is exactly what the US cited when it added its 25% penalty tariff on India in 2025.

A currency war happens when a country deliberately weakens its own currency to make its exports cheaper and imports costlier, gaining a trade advantage without touching a single tariff line. China has faced this accusation repeatedly, most notably when the yuan was allowed to weaken past 7 per US dollar in August 2019, during the US-China trade war, a move many read as retaliation for fresh American tariffs. India is not a currency war participant, but it sits in the blast radius. When global trade tension spikes, capital turns risk-averse and Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) often pull money out of emerging markets like India, which pushes the rupee lower. The RBI then has to choose: intervene by selling dollars from its foreign exchange reserves to defend the INR, or let it depreciate and let a weaker currency absorb part of the shock instead.

body.text: The US is India's single largest export destination, accounting for roughly $80 billion of India's goods exports in FY25, close to a fifth of India's total merchandise exports. A jump in US tariffs is not a rounding error for the Indian economy. It shows up directly in the order books of textile, gems and jewellery, and seafood exporters, and eventually in the earnings of specific Nifty-listed companies with heavy US exposure.

Not every tariff hike is a trade war. Countries adjust tariffs routinely as part of ordinary trade policy. What turns it into a trade war is the retaliation cycle: country A raises a tariff, country B retaliates with its own tariff or restriction, and the exchange escalates instead of settling. Watch for retaliatory language and tit-for-tat announcements, not just the first move.

body.title: Spot the Tool
body.scenario: Country A announces a 20% import duty on solar panels from Country B, citing unfair government subsidies. Two months later, Country B freezes the local bank accounts of three companies from Country A operating within its borders, and separately allows its own currency to depreciate by 8% against the US dollar over the following quarter.
body.prompt: Identify each of the three tools being used in this sequence, and name which country is using which.
body.modelAnswer: Country A used a tariff (the 20% import duty on solar panels). Country B responded with two tools: a sanction-style action (freezing the bank accounts of Country A's companies) and currency policy (allowing an 8% depreciation to make its own exports cheaper and imports costlier). This is a textbook escalation: one tariff answered with both a sanction and a currency move, which is what turns an isolated policy decision into a trade war.

body.title: Which Tool Is This?
body.question: A government bans a foreign telecom company from buying semiconductor chips made anywhere in the world using its technology, and separately blocks the company's local subsidiary from accessing the domestic banking system. Which tool is this?
body.explanation: This is a sanction. It restricts financial and technological access rather than taxing a transaction at the border, and it targets a specific company rather than a product category the way a tariff would.

body.text: A trade war is not a single tariff announcement. It is what happens when tariffs, sanctions, and currency policy stop being used one at a time and start being deployed together, in retaliation, in a rising cycle that neither side fully controls once it starts.

points: Tariffs tax imports at the border and are usually charged as a percentage of a good's value (ad valorem).
Sanctions restrict money, technology, and trading relationships, and target specific countries, banks, or companies rather than product categories.
Currency policy changes the relative price of a whole economy's exports and imports without touching a single tariff line.
India felt all three at once in 2025: a 25% reciprocal US tariff, a 25% penalty tariff tied to Russian oil purchases, and the resulting pressure on FII flows and the rupee.
A trade war is defined by the retaliation cycle, not by any single policy move in isolation.
